'''Harold S.''' "'''Hal'''" '''Johnston'''<ref>The [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] lists Johnston's middle name as ''Sledge'', while his [[National Academy of Sciences]] biographical memoir states that his middle name is ''Siddle''.</ref> (October 11, 1920 – October 20, 2012) was an American scientist who studied [[chemical kinetics]] and [[atmospheric chemistry]]. After beginning his teaching career at [[Stanford University]], he was a faculty member and administrator at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] for nearly 35 years. In 1971, Johnston authored a paper suggesting that environmental pollutants could erode the [[ozone layer]].

Johnston was elected to several scholarly organizations, including the [[National Academy of Sciences]], the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. He won the [[National Medal of Science]] in 1997.

==Early life==
Johnston was born in [[Woodstock, Georgia]], to Florine and Smith Lemon Johnston. His family had been in the area since shortly after the [[Cherokee]] were forced out during the [[Trail of Tears]]. Johnston's paternal grandfather, who had the given name Doctor Medicine Johnston Jr, owned a general store but believed that education was a waste of time. Johnston's father wanted to become a minister, but he could only afford to attend college briefly before acceding to his family's demands to help them run the store.{{sfn|Somorjai|2016|pp=2-4}}

Johnston, who was one of four sons, lived on a Georgia farm when he was young. In the early 1930s, Johnston contracted [[rheumatic fever]] and the illness affected his heart. A physician uncle told Johnston's father not to send Johnston to college because the young man would not survive long enough to get much use out of the education.{{sfn|Somorjai|2016|pp=2-4}} Johnston said he later learned that the disease was associated with an average survival period of fifteen years at the time.<ref name="Nguyen">{{cite news|last1=Nguyen|first1=Andy|title=UC Berkeley chemistry professor Harold Johnston dies at 92|url=http://www.dailycal.org/2012/11/05/uc-berkeley-professor-harold-johnston-dies-at-92/|access-date=October 29, 2016|work=[[The Daily Californian]]|date=November 5, 2012}}</ref> Florine and Smith Johnston valued education for their children, however, and they sent all of their sons to college.{{sfn|Somorjai|2016|pp=2-4}}

After going off to [[Emory University]] with aspirations of becoming a journalist, Johnston soon realized that the U.S. was headed toward [[World War II]] and that a science degree would serve him better.<ref name="Emorymag">{{cite news|last1=Loftus|first1=Mary|title=A pioneer of atmospheric chemistry|url=http://www.emory.edu/EMORY_MAGAZINE/issues/2013/spring/register/tribute.html|access-date=October 29, 2016|work=Emory Magazine|issue=Spring 2013}}</ref> Johnston completed an undergraduate degree in chemistry and a minor in English literature.<ref name="Archive">{{cite web|title=Harold "Hal" Johnston, noted atmospheric chemist and winner of National Medal of Science, has died|url=http://chemistry-archive.berkeley.edu/publications/news/2012/hal-johnston-atmospheric-chemist-has-died.php|publisher=UC Berkeley News Archive|access-date=October 29, 2016|date=November 2, 2012}}</ref> He received a Ph.D. in chemistry and physics from the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref name="Biogr">{{cite journal|title=Biographical notes of Harold Johnston|journal=[[Journal of Physical Chemistry A]]|date=March 1, 2001|volume=105|issue=9|page=1391|doi=10.1021/jp004096v|issn=1089-5639|bibcode=2001JPCA..105.1391.}}</ref> As a doctoral student, Johnston focused on the interaction of [[ozone]] and the pollutant [[nitrogen dioxide]].<ref name="NSTMF">{{cite web|title=Harold S. Johnston|url=https://www.nationalmedals.org/laureates/harold-s-johnston|publisher=[[National Science and Technology Medals Foundation]]|access-date=October 28, 2016}}</ref> While at Caltech, he joined in a secret defense project that involved protecting the country against the use of [[chemical warfare|gas warfare]].<ref name="CEN">{{cite journal|last1=Ainsworth|first1=Susan J.|title=Harold (Hal) Johnston|journal=[[Chemical & Engineering News]]|date=February 25, 2013|volume=91|issue=8|page=44|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/91/i8/Harold-Hal-Johnston.html?type=paidArticleContent|access-date=October 29, 2016}}</ref>

==Career==
From 1947 to 1956, Johnston taught at Stanford University.<ref name="UCS">{{cite web|title=In Memoriam: Harold S. Johnston|url=http://senate.universityofcalifornia.edu/_files/inmemoriam/html/haroldsjohnston.html|publisher=[[University of California]]|access-date=October 28, 2016}}</ref> While there, he was named to the editorial board of the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]''.<ref name="Stanford">{{cite news|title=Stanford chemists win ACS posts|url=http://stanforddailyarchive.com/cgi-bin/stanford?a=d&d=stanford19540210-01.2.7&e=-------en-20--1--txt-txIN-------#|access-date=October 28, 2016|work=[[The Stanford Daily]]|date=February 10, 1954}}</ref> In the early 1950s, Johnston furthered the air pollution work of [[Arie Jan Haagen-Smit]] by showing that [[free-radical reaction]]s underlay the photochemical process leading to smog. Throughout his career, much of Johnston's work involved understanding the kinetics of [[nitrogen oxide]]s.<ref name=Eos/> He returned to Caltech as a faculty member for a year in 1956.<ref name="Eos">{{cite journal|last1=Wuebbles|first1=Donald|title=Harold S. Johnston (1920–2012)|journal=[[Eos (magazine)|Eos, Transactions, American Geophysical Union]]|date=February 26, 2013|volume=94|issue=9|pages=88|doi=10.1002/2013EO090006|language=en|issn=2324-9250|bibcode=2013EOSTr..94...88W}}</ref>

From 1957 until his retirement in 1991, Johnston was a professor at the University of California, Berkeley. From 1966 to 1970, Johnston was the dean of Berkeley's college of chemistry. Johnston mentored undergraduate and graduate students, including future [[Nobel Prize]] winner [[Dudley R. Herschbach]] and future National Medal of Science winner [[Susan Solomon]].<ref name=UCS/> He also made large contributions to the theory of [[elementary reaction|elementary chemical reactions]].<ref name=Eos/> He wrote a popular textbook on reaction rate theory.{{sfn|Somorjai|2016|p=9}}

Johnston became best known for his work related to ozone. In a 1971 paper, he posited that pollution from supersonic aircraft in the stratosphere could deplete the ozone layer.<ref name=NSTMF/> Because it suggested for the first time that human activity could impact the integrity of the environment, Johnston's ozone research received some criticism and resistance.<ref name=NSTMF/> However, two environmental regulatory programs were formed as a result of his findings – the Climatic Impact Assessment Program (CIAP) and the Stratosphere Protection Program.<ref name=NSTMF/>

==Honors and awards==
Johnston was elected a member of the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) in 1965.<ref name=NAS/> He was elected a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1981.<ref name="Bulletin">{{cite journal|title=AAAS elects UC faculty members|journal=University Bulletin: A Weekly Bulletin for the Staff of the University of California|date=March 16, 1981|volume=29|issue=23|page=92|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pvM2AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA92|access-date=October 28, 2016|language=en|last1=(System)|first1=University of California}}</ref>  In 1972, Johnston was elected a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.<ref name="Arts">{{cite web|title=Professor Harold Sledge Johnston|url=https://www.amacad.org/content/system/search.aspx?s=harold+johnston#srConstOverview|publisher=[[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]|access-date=October 28, 2016}}{{Dead link|date=July 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He won the [[Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement]] in 1983.<ref name="Tyler">{{cite web|title=1983 Tyler Laureates|url=http://tylerprize.usc.edu/laureates/tyler1983.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160421125814/http://tylerprize.usc.edu/laureates/tyler1983.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 21, 2016|publisher=[[Tyler Prize for Environmental Achievement]]|access-date=October 28, 2016}}</ref> He received the [[NAS Award for Chemistry in Service to Society]] in 1993.<ref name="NAS">{{cite web|title=Harold Johnston|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/harold-s-johnston-a3tkt6/|website=www.nasonline.org|publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]]|access-date=October 28, 2016}}</ref> Four years later, [[Bill Clinton]] awarded him the National Medal of Science.<ref name=NSTMF/> In 1998, Johnston received the [[Roger Revelle Medal]] from the [[American Geophysical Union]].<ref name="Revelle">{{cite web|title=Roger Revelle Medal|url=http://honors.agu.org/medals-awards/roger-revelle-award/|publisher=[[American Geophysical Union]]|access-date=October 28, 2016|date=3 August 2011}}</ref>

==Later life==
Even in the late 1990s, Johnston said that he had lived most of his life with "a moving 10-year life expectancy" because of his early bout with rheumatic fever, but he remained in good health until he was more than 90 years old.<ref name=Nguyen/> He died in 2012; he was 92. Johnston was survived by his wife of 64 years, Mary Ella, and their four children, as well as several grandchildren and great-grandchildren.<ref name=Archive/>
